elements.quote: Colorectal laterally spreading tumors (LSTs) larger than 20 mm are significant precursors to colorectal cancer. Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) and endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) are widely used treatments, but their comparative efficacy and safety remain controversial.
elements.reason: The text describes the current state of knowledge regarding the treatment of colorectal laterally spreading tumors and identifies the uncertainty regarding the comparative efficacy and safety of ESD and EMR.

elements.quote: Inclusion criteria: (1) Studies involving LSTs with lesions measuring > 20 mm; (2) Comparative studies reporting primary and secondary outcomes of ESD versus EMR. elements.quote: One of the key findings of this meta-analysis is the significant superiority of ESD in reducing recurrence rates of colorectal laterally spreading tumors (LSTs) larger than 20 mm. The overall recurrence rates in the ESD and EMR groups were 0.62% and 12.02%, respectively, which aligns closely with the results of studies such as that by Russo et al. [21]. ... A systematic review and meta-analysis by Chandan et al. demonstrated that STSC after EMR for LSTs > 20 mm significantly lowered adenoma recurrence at the first surveillance colonoscopy (pooled rate: 6%; OR 0.27, p < 0.001) [26]. Similarly, a recent meta-analysis of randomized trials by Santo et al. confirmed that thermal ablation (including both STSC and APC) of post-EMR margins reduced recurrence rates (RR = 0.31, p < 0.001) without increasing the risk of adverse events or delayed bleeding [27].

elements.quote: Therefore, in centers with well-established ESD expertise and experience, ESD should be regarded as the preferred method for the treatment of colorectal LSTs larger than 20 mm, providing superior long-term oncological outcomes (extremely low recurrence rates) while maintaining the safety and efficiency of minimally invasive therapy. For centers at an earlier stage of the ESD learning curve or for selected high-risk cases, EMR remains an important alternative; however, patients should be fully informed of the higher recurrence risk and subject to more intensive surveillance protocols.
